The purpose of this notebook is to allow the NPS team to explore the results
from the sea level rise (SLR) inundation analysis. The data sets were processed
in `rapid_data_processing.Rmd` following the pattern that has been established
for the previous rapid assessment parameters.

The SLR inundation analysis within this notebook concerns itself with exposure.
We are trying to determine what the projected inundation risk of water supplies
of national parks are.

We will start this notebook by pulling in different data sets. We will avoid
generating data here (except for those data manipulations that are necessary for
visualization). 

# Establish environment

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```

```{r}
# Set up work space
source("setup.R")
```

# Load the datasets

You can see how these data sets were generated or loaded in `src/rapid/process_inundation_data.R`

## Read in the water supplies

```{r}
parks <- getParkSystem()

park_centroids <- parks %>% 
  st_centroid() %>% 
  st_transform(4326) %>% 
  dplyr::mutate(y = st_coordinates(.)[,2], x = st_coordinates(.)[,1])
table_path <- "data/Water_Supply_Systems/NPS_Water_Systems_Database_Joined.xlsx"


water_supplies <- read_excel(table_path,
                             sheet = 1,
                             na = c("NA", "U"),
                             skip = 1) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    source_longitude = as.numeric(source_longitude),
    source_latitude = as.numeric(source_latitude)
  ) %>%
  filter(!state %in% c("AK", "AS", "HI", "MP", "PR", "VI")) %>%
  left_join(
    park_centroids %>% 
      st_drop_geometry() %>% 
      dplyr::select(UNIT_CODE, x, y),
    by = c(park_unit = "UNIT_CODE")
  ) %>% dplyr::mutate(
    coords_flag = ifelse(
      is.na(source_longitude) |
        is.na(source_latitude),
      "Centroid",
      "Source Coordinates"
    ),
    source_longitude = ifelse(is.na(source_longitude), x, source_longitude),
    source_latitude = ifelse(is.na(source_latitude), y, source_latitude)
  ) %>%
  # remove municipal and hauled source types, accounting for database entry errors
  filter(!str_detect(source_type, regex("municipal|hauled", ignore_case = TRUE))) %>%
  drop_na(source_longitude, source_latitude) %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = (c("source_longitude", "source_latitude")),
           crs = 4326,
           remove = FALSE)
```

## Read in the SLR inundation exposure risk calculations

You could find how these data were generated in `src/rapid/calc_inundation_exposure.R`.
`calc_inundation_exposure()` function is called in `rapid_workflow.Rmd`.

```{r}
# Buffered water supplies with percent change in inundation
inun_exp_files <- list.files(here("data", "rapid", "outputs"),
                             pattern = "^inundation_exposure_.*\\.csv$",
                             full.names = TRUE)
ws_inun_pct_delta <- read_csv(inun_exp_files[length(inun_exp_files)],
                              show_col_types = FALSE)
```

### Join the percent change dataset with the overall buffered water supply dataset

The buffered water supplies with percent change in inundation dataset only has
those data that were relevant to this analysis. That ends up being about 51 park
units and 384 unique water supplies that were considered for this analysis, and
not all of those had changes.

```{r}
# All buffered water supplies with their percent change
complete_buffered_ws <- left_join(ws_inun_proj_reg, ws_inun_pct_delta,
                                  by = join_by(ID, wsd_source_id, buffer_km, 
                                               inun_proj_mm, inun_proj_closest_mm, 
                                               depth_ft, inun_region, inun_surf_url, 
                                               proj_file, ref_file)) %>%
  mutate(inun_change = ifelse(is.na(inun_change), "no_to_no", inun_change))
```

# Explore...

Now that we have read in all of the data let's explore the analysis.

The data that we used for this analysis is in two parts. The first is the
projected increase in SLR for a region, and the second is the inundation
surfaces that are related to the projected increase in a region. We relate 
both of these data sets to our buffered water supplies.

## Buffered water supplies

The first step was to buffer each water supply point at two distances — 1 km and
4 km — to capture inundation risk both immediately around the source and in its
broader catchment area. The 1 km buffer (black) reflects the near-field risk
directly at the source, while the 4 km buffer (grey) captures the wider area
that could affect it.

```{r}
mapview(all_buffer_ws %>% filter(buffer_km == 4),
        col.regions = "grey",
        alpha.regions = 0.5,
        layer.name = "4 km Buffer") +
  mapview(all_buffer_ws %>% filter(buffer_km == 1),
          col.regions = "black",
          alpha.regions = 0.5,
          layer.name = "1 km Buffer")
```

## Coastal SLR projections

Once the buffers were created, we extracted the projected sea level rise for each
water supply from the Interagency Task Force (ITF) gridded SLR projections (83rd
percentile, 2050). These projections are in millimeters. The full projection
raster covers the entire globe and is too large to visualize directly, so we use
a pre-generated coastal CONUS subset here. Darker areas indicate greater
projected SLR.

```{r}
mapview(coast_projections,
        col.regions = colorRampPalette(c("yellow", "red")),
        na.color = "transparent",
        layer.name = "ITF SLR Projection (mm, 83rd pct, 2050)")
```

## Inundation regions

With the ITF SLR projection value in hand for each water supply, we needed to
match it to the correct NOAA Sea Level Rise Viewer (SLRV) inundation surface.
NOAA's inundation surfaces are organized into geographic regions, each covering
a contiguous coastal area within a state. We determined which region each
buffered water supply fell into using a two-step approach.

**Step 1 — candidate regions:** We spatially joined each buffered water supply
against the bounding boxes of all same-state reference (0 ft SLR) inundation
rasters, keeping every candidate region that intersected the buffer. Sites whose
buffer overlapped only one region proceed directly to the final assignment.

**Step 2 — distance-based disambiguation:** For sites whose buffer intersected
multiple candidate regions, we loaded the reference raster for each candidate
and measured the straight-line distance from the original (unbuffered) water
supply point to the nearest non-NA data cell in that raster. The region whose
raster data lies closest to the water supply point was selected. This ensures
the correct region is chosen even when bounding boxes overlap — a purely
spatial or area-based heuristic can assign a site to a region whose raster has
no actual coverage near that site.

```{r}
mapview(inun_region_bboxs,
        zcol = "state",
        col.regions = colorRampPalette(c("steelblue", "mediumpurple", "darkgreen",
                                         "dodgerblue", "turquoise", "royalblue",
                                         "plum", "seagreen", "cornflowerblue")),
        alpha.regions = 0.3,
        layer.name = "Inundation Region")
```

## Combined view

This map brings together all three components of the processing workflow: the
projected SLR severity across the coast (white to black), the NOAA inundation
regions each water supply was assigned to (colored by state), and the buffered
water supply locations (4 km in orange, 1 km in red). Together these layers show
which water supplies are in high-SLR areas and which inundation surface region
was used to assess their risk.

```{r}
mapview(coast_projections,
        col.regions = colorRampPalette(c("yellow", "red")),
        na.color = "transparent",
        layer.name = "ITF SLR Projection (mm, 83rd pct, 2050)") +
  mapview(inun_region_bboxs,
          zcol = "state",
          col.regions = colorRampPalette(c("steelblue", "mediumpurple", "darkgreen",
                                           "dodgerblue", "turquoise", "royalblue",
                                           "plum", "seagreen", "cornflowerblue")),
          alpha.regions = 0.3,
          layer.name = "Inundation Region") +
  mapview(all_buffer_ws %>% filter(buffer_km == 4),
          col.regions = "grey",
          alpha.regions = 0.5,
          layer.name = "4 km Buffer") +
  mapview(all_buffer_ws %>% filter(buffer_km == 1),
          col.regions = "black",
          alpha.regions = 0.5,
          layer.name = "1 km Buffer")
```

## Understanding the inundation rasters

Before looking at results, it helps to understand what the NOAA inundation
rasters actually contain. Each raster is a binary surface where cells take one
of two states: `1` (inundated at this SLR level), or `NA` (not inundated).

Use the frequency table and map below to verify what NA cells represent in
practice. You will see that the frequency of 1 is the exact difference between
total cells and NA cells.

```{r}
# Load the reference raster for the MD East region as an example
hatu_ref_raw <- terra::rast(here("data", "rapid", "inputs", "coast_comp",
                                  "Extent_Rasters", "MD",
                                  "MD_East_connectRaster_0.tif"))

# Value frequency table: shows counts of 0, 1, and NA
terra::freq(hatu_ref_raw)

# NA cell count
cat("NA cells:", sum(is.na(terra::values(hatu_ref_raw))), "\n")
cat("Total cells:", terra::ncell(hatu_ref_raw), "\n")
cat("Pct NA:", round(sum(is.na(terra::values(hatu_ref_raw))) / terra::ncell(hatu_ref_raw) * 100, 1), "%\n")
```

Here we will map the two data types to verify this assumption again. 
Cells with 1 are displayed in blue, while NA cells are displayed in grey.

```{r}
hatu_ref_viz <- hatu_ref_raw %>%
  terra::trim() %>%
  terra::aggregate(fact = 10, fun = "mean")

mapview(hatu_ref_viz,
        col.regions = "steelblue",
        na.color = "grey",
        layer.name = "NA cells (grey), Inundated cells (blue)")
```

## Understanding the exposure calculation

Now that we have the projected SLR changes and the regions that are specific to
each water supply we can assess the inundation risks.

We did this by taking a count of the pixels in the buffer region around the
water supplies which are inundated under 0 feet of inundation, and comparing
that to their projected inundation surfaces.

Pass an `inun_region` name to `plot_inun_region_exposure()` to see the
reference and projected inundation surfaces for that region alongside the
buffered water supplies. The function zooms to the inundation region bounding
box expanded by 3km.

```{r}
plot_inun_region_exposure <- function(
    inun_region_name,
    ws_data = complete_buffered_ws,
    region_bboxs = inun_region_bboxs,
    raster_dir = here("data", "rapid", "inputs", "coast_comp", "Extent_Rasters")
) {

  if (length(inun_region_name) != 1) {
    stop("Only one inundation region can be plotted at a time.")
  }

  # Filter water supplies to the requested region
  region_ws <- ws_data %>%
    filter(inun_region == inun_region_name)

  if (nrow(region_ws) == 0) {
    stop("No water supplies found for inundation region: ", inun_region_name)
  }

  # Pull raster metadata from the data (one value per region by design)
  state     <- unique(na.omit(region_ws$state))
  ref_file  <- unique(na.omit(region_ws$ref_file))
  proj_file <- unique(na.omit(region_ws$proj_file))

  crs_val <- "+proj=longlat +datum=WGS84 +no_defs"

  # Load, assign CRS, trim, and aggregate reference raster
  ref_rast <- terra::rast(here(raster_dir, state, ref_file))
  terra::crs(ref_rast) <- crs_val
  ref_rast <- ref_rast %>%
    terra::trim() %>%
    terra::aggregate(fact = 10, fun = "mean")

  # Load, assign CRS, trim, and aggregate projected raster
  proj_rast <- terra::rast(here(raster_dir, state, proj_file))
  terra::crs(proj_rast) <- crs_val
  proj_rast <- proj_rast %>%
    terra::trim() %>%
    terra::aggregate(fact = 10, fun = "mean")

  # Build zoom extent: region bbox buffered out 3 km
  ext <- region_bboxs %>%
    filter(inun_region == inun_region_name) %>%
    sf::st_transform(5070) %>%
    sf::st_buffer(3000) %>%
    sf::st_transform(4326) %>%
    sf::st_bbox()

  # Build layered map
  m <- mapview(proj_rast,
               col.regions = "tomato",
               alpha.regions = 0.7,
               na.color = "transparent",
               layer.name = "Projected inundation") +
    mapview(ref_rast,
            col.regions = "steelblue",
            alpha.regions = 0.8,
            na.color = "transparent",
            layer.name = "Reference inundation (0 ft SLR)") +
    mapview(region_ws %>% filter(buffer_km == 4),
            col.regions = "grey",
            alpha.regions = 0.5,
            layer.name = "4 km buffer") +
    mapview(region_ws %>% filter(buffer_km == 1),
            col.regions = "black",
            alpha.regions = 0.5,
            layer.name = "1 km buffer")

  # Zoom to region extent + 3 km buffer
  m@map <- m@map %>%
    leaflet::fitBounds(ext[["xmin"]], ext[["ymin"]], ext[["xmax"]], ext[["ymax"]])

  gc()
  
  return(m)
}
```

Play around here with the plotting function here:

```{r}
plot_inun_region_exposure("MD_Southeast_connectRaster")
```

## Let's get some exciting examples

The dataframes below pull out the most interesting subsets from
`complete_buffered_ws` — top movers by different metrics, and one example each
of the `inun_change` edge cases. Use these data frames to look for interesting
regions to pass into the `plot_inun_region_exposure()` function.

### Biggest raw percent point change

Water supplies with the largest absolute percentage point increase in inundation
coverage (projected minus reference). This is the most intuitive measure of
"how much more of the buffer gets flooded."

```{r}
most_pct_point_change <- complete_buffered_ws %>%
  filter(!is.na(raw_pct_point_change)) %>%
  slice_max(raw_pct_point_change, n = 10) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(park_unit, wsd_source_id, inun_region, buffer_km,
         raw_coverage_pct_ref, raw_coverage_pct_proj, raw_pct_point_change)
```

```{r}
plot_inun_region_exposure(most_pct_point_change$inun_region[1])
```

### Biggest relative percent change

Water supplies with the highest ranked relative percent change. We use
`rank_pct_change` rather than `raw_pct_change` here because `raw_pct_change` is
`Inf` for `no_to_some` sites — the rank handles those correctly by placing them
at the top.

```{r}
most_pct_change <- complete_buffered_ws %>%
  filter(!is.na(rank_pct_change)) %>%
  slice_max(rank_pct_change, n = 10) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(park_unit, wsd_source_id, inun_region, buffer_km,
         raw_coverage_pct_ref, raw_coverage_pct_proj, raw_pct_change, inun_change)
```

```{r}
plot_inun_region_exposure(most_pct_change$inun_region[1])
```

### Biggest absolute cell change

Water supplies with the most raster cells newly flooded in the projected
scenario. Useful for understanding scale of exposure beyond just percentages.

```{r}
most_cell_change <- complete_buffered_ws %>%
  filter(!is.na(raw_cell_change)) %>%
  slice_max(raw_cell_change, n = 10) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(park_unit, wsd_source_id, inun_region, buffer_km,
         raw_flooded_cells_ref, raw_flooded_cells_proj, raw_cell_change)
```

```{r}
plot_inun_region_exposure(most_cell_change$inun_region[1])
```

### `inun_change` category examples

One example of each `inun_change` category — useful for sanity checking the
categorization logic and for building representative visualizations.

```{r}
# No inundation in either scenario — coastal park but not at risk
no_to_no_example <- complete_buffered_ws %>%
  filter(inun_change == "no_to_no") %>%
  slice_head(n = 1)

# Newly inundated — no flooding at reference, some flooding projected
no_to_some_example <- complete_buffered_ws %>%
  filter(inun_change == "no_to_some") %>%
  slice_head(n = 1)

# Worsening inundation — flooded in both scenarios, getting worse
some_to_some_example <- complete_buffered_ws %>%
  filter(inun_change == "some_to_some") %>%
  slice_max(raw_pct_point_change, n = 1)

# Shrinking inundation — flooded at reference, not in projection (edge case)
some_to_no_example <- complete_buffered_ws %>%
  filter(inun_change == "some_to_no") %>%
  slice_head(n = 1)

# Summary of inun_change category counts
complete_buffered_ws %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  count(inun_change, buffer_km)
```

```{r}
plot_inun_region_exposure(some_to_some_example$inun_region[1])
```

# Histogram and result exploration

```{r}
coast_histogram <- function(data, column_name, dataset_name) {
  # Calculate statistics
  stats <- data %>% 
    summarise(
      n = sum(!is.na(.data[[column_name]])),
      min = min(.data[[column_name]], na.rm = TRUE),
      q1 = quantile(.data[[column_name]], 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
      median = median(.data[[column_name]], na.rm = TRUE), 
      q3 = quantile(.data[[column_name]], 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
      max = max(.data[[column_name]], na.rm = TRUE)
    )
  
  # Format summary for display
  summary_text <- paste0(
    "n = ", scales::comma(stats$n), "\n",
    "Min: ", scales::comma(round(stats$min, 1)), "\n",
    "Q1: ", scales::comma(round(stats$q1, 1)), "\n", 
    "Median: ", scales::comma(round(stats$median, 1)), "\n",
    "Q3: ", scales::comma(round(stats$q3, 1)), "\n",
    "Max: ", scales::comma(round(stats$max, 1))
  )
  
  # Determine if log scale needed (high skew)
  use_log <- (stats$max / stats$median) > 100 && stats$median > 0
  
  p <- ggplot(data, aes(x = .data[[column_name]])) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "#2C3E50", alpha = 0.8, color = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = c(stats$median, stats$q1, stats$q3), 
               color = c("#E74C3C", "#F39C12", "#F39C12"), 
               linewidth = c(1.2, 0.8, 0.8),
               linetype = c("solid", "dashed", "dashed")) +
    annotate("text", x = Inf, y = Inf, label = summary_text,
             hjust = 1.05, vjust = 1.05, size = 3.5, family = "serif",
             color = "#2C3E50",
             bbox = list(boxstyle = "round,pad=0.4", facecolor = "white", 
                         edgecolor = "#BDC3C7", linewidth = 0.5)) +
    labs(
      title = str_to_title(gsub("_", " ", column_name)),
      subtitle = paste("Dataset:", dataset_name),
      x = NULL, y = "Count"
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      text = element_text(family = "serif", color = "#2C3E50"),
      plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, hjust = 0.5, color = "#7F8C8D"),
      axis.text = element_text(size = 10),
      axis.title.y = element_text(size = 11),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.x = element_line(color = "#ECF0F1", linewidth = 0.3),
      panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "#ECF0F1", linewidth = 0.3)
    )
  
  # Apply log scale if needed
  if (use_log) {
    p <- p + scale_x_log10(labels = scales::comma_format())
  } else {
    p <- p + scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma_format())
  }
  
  return(p)
}

# Key metrics to explore — raw values and their normalized counterparts.
# raw_pct_change is excluded here because it contains Inf for no_to_some sites;
# use rank_pct_change instead to get a well-behaved distribution.
key_metrics <- c(
  "raw_coverage_pct_ref",  "raw_coverage_pct_proj",
  "raw_pct_point_change",  "raw_cell_change",
  "norm_coverage_pct_ref", "norm_coverage_pct_proj",
  "norm_pct_point_change", "norm_cell_change",
  "rank_pct_change"
)

# Waters with changes only: exclude no_to_no rows whose raw metrics are all NA
changes_only <- ws_inun_pct_delta %>%
  filter(inun_change != "no_to_no")

# Build one histogram per metric for each dataset
changes_plots <- map(key_metrics, function(metric) {
  coast_histogram(changes_only, metric, "Waters with Changes Only")
})
names(changes_plots) <- key_metrics

all_ws_plots <- map(key_metrics, function(metric) {
  coast_histogram(complete_buffered_ws %>% st_drop_geometry(), metric, "All Water Supplies")
})
names(all_ws_plots) <- key_metrics

# Display each metric as a side-by-side comparison
comparison_plots <- map(key_metrics, function(metric) {
  changes_plots[[metric]] + all_ws_plots[[metric]] +
    plot_layout(ncol = 2) +
    plot_annotation(
      title = paste("Comparison:", str_to_title(gsub("_", " ", metric))),
      theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5))
    )
})
names(comparison_plots) <- key_metrics
```

`inun_change` is categorical so it gets its own bar chart rather than a
histogram. Counts are broken out by buffer size so you can see whether the
1 km and 4 km buffers tell different stories.

```{r}
complete_buffered_ws %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(!is.na(inun_change)) %>%
  count(inun_change, buffer_km) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = inun_change, y = n, fill = factor(buffer_km))) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("1" = "red", "4" = "orange"),
                    labels = c("1" = "1 km", "4" = "4 km"),
                    name = "Buffer") +
  labs(
    title = "Inundation Change Categories",
    subtitle = "Count of water supplies by category and buffer size",
    x = NULL, y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    text = element_text(family = "serif", color = "#2C3E50"),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, hjust = 0.5, color = "#7F8C8D"),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10)
  )
```
